svg.title: An eight member link bundle carrying one flow on one member, and the hash inputs and traffic patterns that decide whether the aggregate is usable
svg.desc: A bundle of eight ten gigabit members. One red flow arrives and is placed on a single member, giving ten gigabits per second, while many green flows spread across six members. Below, the hash inputs are compared: Layer 2 addresses distribute poorly for routed traffic, Layer 3 addresses are better but a single host pair still forms one flow, and Layer 3 plus Layer 4 ports distribute best. A table on the right maps common traffic patterns to the bandwidth they can actually reach, including backup and live migration limited to one member and server farms reaching near the aggregate. A note at the bottom explains case 3: eight ten gigabit links promised eighty gigabits and delivered twelve, because the workload used two flows.
svg.text: Aggregate bandwidth is a property of the bundle; usable bandwidth is a property of the flow
Eight members, one hash, and no mechanism anywhere that reorders a single conversation
8 × 10 Gb/s members
one flow → one member → 10 Gb/s
a single conversation cannot be reordered
one TCP flow
six flows → six members → up to 60 Gb/s
utilisation follows the flow mix, not the ordering
many conversations, each hashed to one member for its lifetime
THE HASH INPUT DECIDES THE DISTRIBUTION
Layer 2 only
poor for routed traffic: every packet has the same router MACs
Layer 3
better across servers, still one flow between one host pair
Layer 3 + Layer 4
best: many sessions between the same hosts spread out
Change the hash only after measuring; it changes every existing distribution at once.
TRAFFIC PATTERN → WHAT YOU ACTUALLY GET
Backup and replication
one or two large flows → one member → 10 Gb/s, with the rest idle
Live migration
one flow per migration → one member; concurrent moves help
Server farm, many clients
hundreds of flows → close to the aggregate, hash quality permitting
Video distribution
many receivers, few sources: good, if the sources differ
Storage over Ethernet
measured, not assumed: some vendors pin flows to a member
The number to promise in a design document is per flow, and it
is always one member. Everything above that is statistical.
If the business case depends on aggregate bandwidth, the
business case depends on a measurement nobody has taken.
Two ways out: more flows (application), or fewer, faster links.
Case 3 in this chapter is this figure with a purchase order attached: eight ten gigabit links, an eighty gigabit promise, and a measured twelve.
Nobody lied and nothing failed. The workload had two flows, the hash placed them on two members, and the other six members carried monitoring traffic.
Ask for the flow count before you buy the aggregate. If the answer is "we do not know", the honest design is one faster link plus one for redundancy — and a measurement plan.
Write the difference into the acceptance document, in one sentence, before the hardware arrives.
